title: A Wellness & Healing Tour of Korea: 2 Nights, 3 Days for First-Timers
html:
Most "wellness trip" articles about Korea point you to a luxury hotel spa. This itinerary is different — it's built around the everyday wellness habits Koreans actually use: the neighborhood jjimjilbang (public bathhouse), a visit to a traditional herbal medicine market, and a quiet morning at a mountain temple known for its food. None of it requires a resort budget, a car, or any prior experience — just comfortable clothes and a little patience with the unfamiliar.

This is a 2-night, 3-day plan that stays inside Seoul the whole time, so you can slot it into a longer trip without extra travel days.

Day 1: Unwind at a Real Korean Spa (Jjimjilbang)


Spa Lei, a women-only jjimjilbang (Korean public bathhouse and sauna) in Seocho-gu, Seoul. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

A jjimjilbang is a Korean public bathhouse and sauna, usually open 24 hours. There are two very different zones inside, and knowing this before you go will save you some confusion:

  • The bathing area: gender-separated, and yes — everyone bathes without clothes here. This is completely normal in Korea and nobody will stare; it's treated the same way a locker room is. If you're not ready for that part, it's fine to skip it.
  • The sauna and relaxation floors: mixed-gender (in most jjimjilbang), and you wear the cotton uniform the front desk gives you. This is where people nap on heated floors, watch TV, get a snack, or sit in themed heat rooms (salt rooms, charcoal rooms, ice rooms).

For this itinerary, we're using Spa Lei in Seocho-gu (near Gangnam-daero), a well-known women-only spa with a calm, slightly European-style interior, hot tubs, and herbal saunas. It's open 24 hours, and entry (which includes your uniform) is roughly ₩16,000–25,000 for about half a day — prices and exact hourly limits do change, so check current pricing before you go. If you're traveling as a couple or a mixed group, look up a co-ed jjimjilbang instead, such as Dragon Hill Spa in Yongsan, which is one of the most visited by foreign travelers.

💡 How locals actually do it: For most Koreans, a jjimjilbang isn't a luxury treat — it's a cheap, normal way to relax on a weekend, and some even use the overnight sleeping floor as a backup place to crash after a late train instead of booking a hotel room. Bring your own toothbrush if you plan to stay a while; not every location provides one.

Day 2 Morning: Exploring Gyeongdong Herbal Medicine Market


Gyeongdong Market, Seoul's best-known traditional market for dried herbs, ginseng, and oriental medicine ingredients. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Gyeongdong Market (near Jegi-dong, Dongdaemun-gu — closest station is Jegidong on Line 1) has been Seoul's main hub for dried herbs, ginseng, and hanbang (traditional Korean medicine) ingredients since it opened in 1960. Even if you have no interest in buying anything, it's worth an hour of wandering: stalls are piled high with dried mushrooms, cinnamon bark, ginseng roots, and sacks of herbs you've probably never seen before, and vendors are used to curious visitors.

Make time to stop at "Gyeongdong 1960" — a Starbucks built inside the market's old 1960s theater, which had been closed and empty since 1994. The renovated building keeps the original curved balcony and stage area, so you're drinking coffee inside a piece of the market's history. It's on the 3rd–4th floor inside the market complex, and it's a popular enough photo spot that you may want to go earlier in the day to get a seat.

💡 How locals actually do it: Many Korean visitors come specifically to buy a season's supply of hong-sam (red ginseng) or herbal tea packets for their own family rather than for a single souvenir — it's normal to see people buying in bulk here, not just a small bag.

Day 2 Afternoon: A Hanbang (Traditional Medicine) Clinic Visit


Choi Hyeok Korean Medicine Clinic, located inside the Yangnyeongsi herbal medicine district next to Gyeongdong Market. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Hanbang is the umbrella term for Korean traditional medicine — things like acupuncture, herbal tonics (hanyak), and pulse-based consultations with a licensed practitioner. Right next to Gyeongdong Market, the Yangnyeongsi district is full of small hanbang clinics, and Choi Hyeok Korean Medicine Clinic is one that's used to seeing foreign visitors (it's especially popular with Japanese tourists) and offers short consultations, acupuncture, and custom herbal tonics.

You don't need to be sick to try this — many visitors go just for a short consultation and a cup of herbal tea, or to have a custom tonic made up that can be shipped to your hotel or home. Call ahead to check availability and whether English support is on hand that day, since staffing changes, and treat any health claims you hear here the way you would at any clinic abroad — as a cultural experience, not a substitute for your own doctor.

💡 How locals actually do it: Visiting a hanbang clinic in autumn or winter for a seasonal "boyak" (tonic) is a pretty normal habit for a lot of Korean families, almost like a flu-season vitamin routine — it's treated as everyday self-care, not an alternative medicine statement.

Day 3: Temple Food and Forest Air at Jingwansa


Jingwansa Temple, one of the four major temples surrounding Seoul, set in the forest at the foot of Bukhansan. Photo: Korea Tourism Organization (data.go.kr TourAPI).

Spend your last morning at Jingwansa Temple, tucked into the forest at the foot of Bukhansan in Eunpyeong-gu. It's one of the four traditional temples that historically guarded the approaches to Seoul, and today it's known across Korea for its temple food — simple, vegetable-based monastic cooking that became internationally famous after being featured on Netflix's Chef's Table. Just walking the grounds, past halls like Daeungjeon and Nahanjeon, with the quiet of the mountain forest around you, is the "healing" part of this trip — no program required.

To get there: take subway Line 3 to Gupabal Station, Exit 1, then a short bus ride or taxi (around 10 minutes) to the temple. The grounds are open 09:00–18:00 and free to simply visit. If you'd rather have the full experience, Jingwansa also runs an official templestay program (a day program or an overnight stay), which typically costs somewhere between ₩50,000 and ₩100,000 depending on length — book through the official templestay.com site, ideally 3–4 weeks ahead, since this temple fills up fast. Afterward, walk over to the nearby Eunpyeong Hanok Village for a relaxed lunch before heading back into the city.

💡 How locals actually do it: Most Koreans visit temples like this for quiet, not for religion — a weekday afternoon walk through the grounds is a common way to reset before a busy week, and weekdays are also noticeably less crowded than weekends if you want it even quieter.

Here's a quick recap of the three main stops, in case you're short on time and need to pick just one or two:

ExperienceApprox. costTime neededBooking needed?Best for
Jjimjilbang (Spa Lei)₩16,000–25,0002–4 hours (or overnight)No — walk inRelaxing, budget-friendly, trying real Korean bathhouse culture
Gyeongdong Market + hanbang clinicFree to browse; clinic visit varies2–3 hoursClinic: call aheadCurious shoppers, anyone wanting a short cultural consultation
Jingwansa TempleFree to visit; ₩50,000–100,000 for templestayHalf day (or overnight)Templestay: yes, weeks aheadQuiet, nature, and famous temple food

🌿 Curious about trying any of these — especially the jjimjilbang part? Ask away in the comments, I'm happy to walk you through what to expect!
meta_description: A beginner's 2N3D Korea wellness itinerary: a real jjimjilbang spa, Gyeongdong herbal market, a hanbang clinic, and temple food at Jingwansa.
